title: The What-If Scenario Lab
goal: Your kid takes a big what-if, like a week with no electricity, and thinks it all the way through. They map what would really happen, find someone who has lived something like it, make a plan, try a small slice of it for real, then handle a twist and convince the family.
need: Someone to ask who has lived something like it
A few hours to try a small slice for real
Books or the internet for looking things up (optional)

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You don't need any expertise. Your job is to wonder alongside them, take every idea seriously, and keep asking 'And then what?' Share what you'd worry about too. Good what-ifs happen at the supper table and in the car, and then one evening you try a piece of it for real.

plan.what: Pick a what-if and map what would happen (Steps 1 and 2).
Ask someone who knows, and make the plan (Steps 3 and 4).
Try a slice, handle a twist and convince the family (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.a: Pick a playful one, like Ten things or Kids in charge. Finish by asking what might be better in that world.
Say 'And then what?' three times in a row. Or go first, and share your own answer badly.
Great. Don't correct them. Ask 'How would that work on Day 3?' and let the plan test itself.

lesson.text: A good what-if answer doesn't stop at the first idea. It keeps going: and then what, and then what, and who does that affect?
lesson.before: If there was no electricity, we'd use flashlights.

The food's going bad and the phones are dead.

lesson.modelNote: The first answer solved the first hour. The second kept going, ran into a hard choice and then got tested for real.

steps.title: Choose your what-if
steps.why: The best question is the one they can't stop thinking about.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a question from the What-ifs card in the Lab Toolkit at the end of the guide, or invents their own. They say their very first reaction out loud or on paper, before thinking too hard.
steps.you: Give your own first reaction too. Then ask what makes it hard, and not just different.
ask: What's the first thing you thought of?
What would you miss the most?
steps.tip: Write the first reaction down and keep it. It's fun to compare at the end.

levels.explore: Pick one what-if and say or draw what you'd do first.
levels.develop: Pick two and name the biggest problem in each.
levels.extend: Pick three, rank them from easiest to hardest, and defend the order.

steps.title: Map what would happen
steps.why: The first day is easy. Day 3 is where it gets interesting.
steps.kid: Your kid walks through it day by day, using the Keep asking card: what changes first, what gets harder by Day 3 and Day 7, who it's hardest for and what people would argue about. They add a line every time someone says 'And then what?'
steps.you: Ask about the things they haven't thought of yet, like the neighbours, the pets, the grandparents. Say 'Here's what I'd worry about' and add one of your own.
ask: What problem would show up that most people wouldn't think of?
Who would this be hardest for?
steps.tip: Draw three columns: Day 1, Day 3, Day 7. It's a lot easier to see the problems pile up.

levels.explore: Name three things that would change in the first week.
levels.develop: Map the problems across Day 1, Day 3 and Day 7.
levels.extend: Build a timeline with practical problems, feelings and who'd disagree about what.

steps.title: Ask someone who knows
steps.why: Somebody has already lived some version of this.
steps.kid: Your kid finds out how real people have handled something like it. Best of all, they ask someone: a grandparent who remembers a long power cut, a neighbour who grew up on a farm, a friend who moved countries. Then they write down what surprised them.
steps.you: Help them think of who to ask, and make the call or visit together. Look things up with them if there's no one to ask.
ask: What did they do that you wouldn't have thought of?
What was the hardest part for them?
steps.tip: Ask 'What did you not expect?' It gets better stories than 'What happened?'

levels.explore: Ask one person, or find one story, and share what you learned.
levels.develop: Ask one person and find two facts, and say how each changes your thinking.
levels.extend: Compare two real examples from different places, and work out why people handled them differently.

steps.title: Make the plan, then try a slice
steps.why: A plan on paper has never had to make supper.
steps.kid: Your kid writes what you'd do on Day 1, how you'd handle the biggest problems and what you'd have to give up. Then they pick a small slice from the Try a slice card and you all live it for a few hours, and fix the plan with what you learned.
steps.you: Ask 'What about...?' to find the gaps, and then really do the slice. No cheating, for the agreed time. Use flashlights rather than candles, and keep the safety rules you always have.
ask: If two important things clash, which one wins?
steps.tip: Keep the slice short, and pick a real start and end time. A few hours is plenty to feel it.

levels.explore: Make a five-step plan for the first day, and try the slice with your family.
levels.develop: Plan for each big problem, name a trade-off, try the slice and change one thing.
levels.extend: Plan for the first week, the first month and beyond, name three trade-offs, and use the slice to test your riskiest idea.

steps.title: Handle the twist and convince the family
steps.why: A plan isn't finished until someone tries to poke a hole in it.
steps.kid: You throw a twist from the Twists card and your kid changes the plan. Then they fill in Our plan at the end of the guide and present it to the family as if everyone had to live by it. They answer every doubt, and compare it with their first reaction.
steps.you: Be the toughest person in the room, kindly. Ask 'Why should I agree to that?' Then tell them which part convinced you.
ask: Does this twist break the plan or only stretch it?
How is your thinking different from the start?
steps.tip: Read their first reaction out loud at the end. It's usually very funny, and a good way to see how far they've come.

levels.explore: Hear one twist, say what you'd change, and tell the family your plan.
levels.develop: Handle two twists, fill in Our plan and answer the family's questions.
levels.extend: Handle every twist at once, then present a final version with your evidence and your trade-offs.

conclusion.headline: They didn't stop at the first answer.
conclusion.text: Listen for it over the next few weeks. If they say 'But then what would happen?' about something in the news, a family plan or a story they're reading, the habit is sticking.
conclusion.celebrate: At the end, read their first reaction beside the final plan and say: 'Look how far you took that.'

signs: They ask what happens next instead of stopping at the first answer

makeItReal: Keep a running list of what-ifs on the fridge, and take one out at supper once a week.
